summary: Ethereum tanked yesterday following the news of Binance security breach, which reportedly resulted in approximately $6.3 billion being drained from wallets across multiple blockchains. It was the largest cryptocurrency heist in history. The hack raised concerns about exchange security and potential contagion across the crypto ecosystem. Although Binance pledged to cover customer losses, uncertainty surrounding the stolen assets and potential liquidations weighed on sentiment. Around $1.53 billion in leveraged positions were liquidated over 24 hours. While the Binance hack triggered the initial shock, leveraged positioning and cascading liquidations magnified the losses. Historically, cryptocurrency selloffs triggered by exchange hacks have often been followed by a recovery, but the economic context decided how quickly. The initial reaction tends to be driven by panic, uncertainty and forced liquidations rather than a deterioration in the fundamentals of cryptocurrencies. The macro picture is still largely bearish given inflation risks, growth concerns, risk-off sentiment, upcoming rate hikes and geopolitical tensions. A significant improvement in risk sentiment is likely needed to change the current trend. Possible catalysts include a breakthrough in US-Iran negotiations and dovish Fed comments. title: US employment cost index for Q3 +0.8% vs +0.8% expected
summary: Prior quarter was +0.9% Employment benefits +0.9% vs +1.0% prior quarter Employment wages +0.7% vs +0.9% prior quarter The US Employment Cost Index (ECI) increased by 0.8% q/q in the third quarter, with both wages and salaries and benefit costs contributing to the increase. Wages and salaries rose 0.7%, while benefit costs increased 0.9% compared with the previous quarter. On an annual basis, total compensation costs for civilian workers increased by 3.4%, with wages and salaries rising 3.1% and benefit costs accelerating by 3.9%. The figures show that labour cost pressures remain relatively contained, although benefits continue to increase faster than wages. Looking at private industry, compensation costs also increased by 0.8% q/q and 3.4% y/y. However, inflation-adjusted wages and salaries declined by 0.6% over the year, as nominal wage growth is still failing to keep pace with consumer price increases. The continued gap between nominal and inflation-adjusted wage growth also highlights the pressure households are facing from higher living costs. For background, the Employment Cost Index (ECI) is a quarterly report from the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) that measures the change in the total cost of labor for businesses. The Fed considers the ECI the "gold standard" for measuring wage inflation because it is more precise and comprehensive, the only drawback is that it's not as timely as the Average Hourly Earnings data. title: Italy October preliminary CPI +5.4% vs +4.6% y/y expected
summary: Prior +4.2% HICP +5.6% vs +4.6% y/y expected Prior +4.2% Inflation accelerated sharply in October 2026, but the increase was primarily driven by energy prices, with both regulated and non-regulated energy products recording significant increases. Regulated energy inflation surged from 25.8% to 59.5% y/y, while non-regulated energy prices accelerated from 22.5% to 29.4%. Higher energy costs remain the dominant driver of the inflationary shock. However, price pressures were not limited to energy. Unprocessed food inflation accelerated from 5.5% to 7.5%, while processed food prices also returned to positive annual growth. Services inflation picked up more modestly, rising to 2.9% from 2.6%, with transport-related services accelerating to 3.1%. The goods component was particularly notable, with annual inflation jumping to 7.5% from 5.4%, while services inflation remained considerably more contained. This suggests that the latest acceleration is still heavily concentrated in goods and energy-related costs rather than reflecting an equally broad-based increase across the services sector. Overall, the data points to significant inflationary shock in Italy, largely driven by surging energy costs but increasingly spilling over into food and transportation prices. This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

In any case, just keep in mind though that the state readings aren't a perfect proxy for the national figure. There can still be some deviation when the preliminary numbers are released later. title: Spain Q3 GDP growth slows slightly but it's the inflation problem that should worry the ECB
summary: Spain Q3 preliminary GDP +0.6% vs +0.6% q/q expected Prior +0.7% Spain Q3 preliminary GDP +2.7% vs +2.7% y/y expected Prior +2.6% It is the preliminary report, so there aren't much details to work with here besides the headline figures above. The quarterly figure does show a bit of a slowdown in Spanish economic growth in the third quarter, albeit marginally. And among the bigger names in the euro area, Spain is still very much punching above its weight in carrying the more optimistic banner for the region. The only issue is that inflation pressures in Spain is also starting to get out of hand . Headline annual inflation is bordering on 5% in October with core annual inflation holding above 3%. Those numbers are way beyond what the ECB would be comfortable with, running above their 2% price target. The Spanish GDP report here isn't something to spook markets. But a mild slowdown if coupled with troubling performances in France and perhaps Germany later, that could really ramp up talk of stagflation risks in the euro area especially when paired with the inflation numbers today. Traders might still lean more favourably on inflation risks prompting the ECB to act in December. But if growth conditions continue to suffer, it might only be a matter of time before the narrative shifts and the focus turns to stagflation risks instead. So, just be wary of that. This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

title: Spain inflation remains stubbornly high near 5% as the ECB headache gets worse
summary: Spain October preliminary CPI +4.9% vs +4.9% y/y expected Prior +4.9% Spain October preliminary HICP +4.9% vs +4.9% y/y expected Prior +5.0% Spanish inflation continues to hover around 5% in October, as the preliminary estimates continue to paint a rather uncomfortable picture for the most part. Headline annual inflation remains steady at 4.9% while the harmonised reading eased marginally to 4.9% as well. So, that's not saying a lot after the run higher in the past few months amid a surge energy prices due to the Middle East conflict. And with higher oil prices continuing to stick, that will certainly add to the inflation headache in Q4. Looking at the details, core annual inflation is seen at 3.1% - unchanged compared to September. But at this level, it is still well above what the ECB would be comfortable with as price pressures continue to pull away from the 2% target. Alongside the earlier report from France, this just continues to reaffirm that the inflation monster is getting bigger and more threatening for the central bank. But at the same time, flagging economic growth conditions will just mean that stagflation risks are also on the rise. So, that is quite a troubling spot for policymakers to be in as they have to try and deal with price pressures before they get out of hand while avoiding sending the broader economy off a cliff. Tough. This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

title: France inflation heats up again in October, leaving the ECB caught between a rock and a hard place
summary: France October preliminary CPI +3.4% vs +3.2% y/y expected Prior +3.1% France October preliminary HICP +3.8% vs +3.6% y/y expected Prior +3.4% French inflation is seen accelerating again in October, as the preliminary estimates show headline annual inflation climbing to its highest since December 2023. Yowza. The main culprit is once again energy prices, as that continues to fuel much of the headline price increase. No pun intended. Of note, energy price inflation was up 24.1% annually in October compared to 21.3% in the month before. The detailed breakdown shows food price inflation softening slightly to 1.2% in October but services inflation is seen picking up further to 2.7% from 2.4% in the month before. The latter is a real issue as it signals that higher energy prices are starting to spill over more broadly, and that will in turn feed into core inflation as well. It's not a good look if you're the ECB. France is already struggling economically, not to mention with fiscal headwinds growing stronger by the day. And with inflation pressures starting to heat up as well, that is making for a very stagflationary outlook for Europe's second-largest economy. For the central bank, this is their biggest issue and risk to tightening policy further. That is especially the case as French bonds are also coming under heavy pressure amid fiscal worries and that could threaten to blow over to the rest of the euro area as well.
